quotes.text: for over forty years Thomas Jamison and Mary A. Jamison, husband and wife, lived together in the house No. 351 Forty-sixth street, in the borough of Brooklyn, where they eked out a livelihood by renting furnished rooms.
in and about the renting, cleaning, management and care of the premises No. 351 46th Street, Borough of Brooklyn, City of New York, as a house with furnished rooms for lodgers.

court: New York Supreme Court, Appellate Division
holding_summary: In a wife's suit for separation, the court found that the wife had taken a boarder and let a furnished room to supplement household income, which the husband wished to stop; the court held that a husband who maintains the family has the right to decide who resides in the home and may refuse to permit boarders, and that his objection did not amount to cruelty, so the separation judgment was reversed and the complaint dismissed.

quotes.text: To eke out the income the wife took a boarder and let out a furnished room.

But the husband who maintains the family has a right to say who shall reside with them in the home, and may refuse to have boarders whose requirements interfere with the family comfort and whose presence excites comment on the part of the neighbors.

notes: Letting a boarder/furnished room by a householder to supplement income is treated as an unremarkable, lawful practice (favorable); but the holding restrains the wife's continuation of it via the husband's domestic authority, not police-power regulation (hence mixed). duration_of_occupancy unclear -- no term specified for the boarder's stay.

court: New York Supreme Court, Appellate Division
holding_summary: A restrictive covenant limiting use of villa lots to buildings 'used or occupied ... as a private dwelling house or habitation' was held to exclude hotel/inn use; defendant's conversion of his building into a 24-bedroom hotel with a bar violated the covenant, and the court enjoined use of the building for any purpose other than a private dwelling.

quotes.text: Private dwelling houses do not include an inn or a hotel.
put another story upon the building and, in his own words, made “a first class hotel of it.”
the judgment must be amended so as to restrain the defendants from using the building or permitting it to be used for any purpose other than a private dwelling

notes: Adverse in the sense relevant to the corpus: commercial paid-guest lodging (a hotel with 24 bedrooms, bar service) is sustained as legally distinct from and excluded by a 'private dwelling' restriction, i.e. treated as a commercial intrusion into a residential covenant scheme.
